Born in Tokyo, Japan, Emily graduated from Tufts University and the Graduate School of Journalism at the University of California at Berkeley.

Emily Taguchi will be a panelist on the When No One Else is Watching panel.

speakers.name: Karim Amer
speakers.bio: Karim is an Academy Award-nominated filmmaker. He has recently produced and directed the upcoming Showtime docu-series focusing on the scandal-ridden Lincoln Project, and Flight / Risk, a new documentary around Boeing’s controversial 737 Max planes, for Amazon Studios. He produced and directed THE VOW (2020), a series about the self-improvement group NXIVM. THE GREAT HACK (2019) premiered at the Sundance Film Festival, made the Academy Award and Grierson shortlist, was BAFTA-nominated, Emmy-nominated, and won a Cinema Eye Award. He produced the Golden Globe-winning series RAMY (2019) and teamed up with Angelina Jolie to produce Academy Award-nominated THE BREADWINNER (2017). He also produced Emmy-winning and Oscar-nominated THE SQUARE (2013), Audience Award-winner at the Sundance Film Festival and the Toronto Film Festival, and RAFEA: SOLAR MAMA (2013). Karim is a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.

speakers.name: Edward Baker
speakers.bio:
Edward Baker is Of Counsel in Constantine Cannon’s Washington, D.C. office. He represents a broad range of whistleblowers and has extensive experience, in particular, with healthcare and defense procurement fraud under the federal False Claims Act and equivalent state acts. Prior to joining Constantine Cannon, Mr. Baker was an Assistant U.S. Attorney in the Eastern District of California within the Affirmative Civil Enforcement practice group. He previously served as the Director of the Vermont Medicaid Fraud Control Unit (MFCU), prosecuting civil and criminal Medicaid fraud cases. He began his professional career in private practice in government enforcement defense, commercial litigation, and plaintiff-side class actions.

Edward will be featured in the Pro Bono Legal Clinic.

speakers.name: Tina Rosenberg
speakers.bio:
Tina Rosenberg is co-writer of the New York Times Fixes column and co-founder of the Solutions Journalism Network. She is a longtime New York Times writer, for the editorial page and Sunday magazine as well as Fixes. She has written hundreds of magazine articles for publications such as The New Yorker, The Atlantic and Rolling Stone as well as the Times Sunday magazine. She has also written three books: Children of Cain: Violence and the Violent in Latin America; The Haunted Land: Facing Europe’s Ghosts After Communism; and Join the Club: How Peer Pressure Can Transform the World. She won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award for Haunted Land.

Tina Rosenberg will be a facilitator on the Solutions Journalism for Investigative Film workshop.

speakers.name: Claire Wardle
speakers.bio:
Claire Wardle leads the strategic direction and research for First Draft. In 2009 she left her academic position at Cardiff University to develop an organization wide training program for the BBC on social media, verification and misinformation and has been obsessed with the topic ever since. In 2017 she co-authored the seminal report, Information Disorder: An interdisciplinary Framework for Research and Policy for the Council of Europe. Over the past decade she has been a Fellow at the Shorenstein Center for Media, Politics and Public Policy at Harvard’s Kennedy School, the Research Director at the Tow Center for Digital Journalism at Columbia University’s Graduate School of Journalism and head of social media for the United Nations Refugee Agency. She holds a Ph.D. in Communication from the University of Pennsylvania.

clairewardle.com

Claire will be presenting on the Playbook for a Pandemic: Disinformation in the Age of COVID-19 panel.

speakers.name: Jay Rosen
speakers.bio:
Jay Rosen has been teaching journalism at New York University since 1986. He is the author of PressThink, a blog about journalism and its ordeals (www.pressthink.org), which he introduced in September 2003. In 1999, Yale University Press published his book, What Are Journalists For?, which is about the rise of the civic journalism movement during the pre-internet era. In 2017 he became director of the Membership Puzzle Project, funded by the Knight Foundation, Democracy Fund, and Luminate. It studies membership models for sustainability in the news. Rosen is also an active press critic with a focus on problems in the coverage of politics.

Jay Rosen will be a panelist on The New Transparency panel.

speakers.name: Marika Adair
speakers.bio:
Marika Adair is the Festival Manager at the Double Exposure Investigative Film Festival and Symposium. Previously she held the position of Executive & Programming Director for the Visions Film Festival & Conference, which is where her love of film festivals and event management originated. She believes that film festivals have the opportunity to bring forth change and make a difference in a world that desperately needs it. She hopes to one day run a film festival in her hometown of Wilkesboro, NC, where she can give back to the community and share her love for film and media.

Marika spends her free time taking photos and creating her own short films, which vary in subject and form but are mainly just for fun. She enjoys many other forms of entertainment, from music videos to podcasts to just enjoying the great outdoors. She holds a Bachelor’s in Film Studies from the University of North Carolina Wilmington.

speakers.name: Isabelle Di Rita
speakers.bio:
[vc_row][vc_column][vc_column_text]Isabelle Di Rita is writer and filmmaker from Washington, D.C. studying Literary Arts at Brown University (’20).

She has written & directed several short films and most recently wrote, directed, and produced a mini-musical for the Brown Musical Forum, Imagical, based on the life of J.K. Rowling.

In 2018-2019 she worked as a staff member for the Ivy Film Festival (IFF), the largest international student-run film festival. Next year she will serve as an IFF Event Coordinator[/vc_column_text][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row][vc_column][vc_btn title=”Contact information” style=”custom” custom_background=”#99ff33″ custom_text=”#000000″ shape=”square” size=”lg” link=”url:mailto%3Amarga%40dxfest.com|||” el_class=”btn”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row][vc_column][vc_empty_space height=”12px”][vc_column_text]isabelle@doubleexposurefestival-com.lyricalstaging.com[/vc_column_text][/vc_column][/vc_row]

speakers.name: Marga Varea
speakers.bio:
Marga Varea is the founder of Twin Seas Media, a Boston-based impact distribution boutique agency working with documentary films and documentary film festivals. With over twenty years of experience in film and television, Marga has a deep understanding of the industry and believes in the power of storytelling to engage, educate and transform. Marga has worked with dozens of documentary films and film festivals over the years in a variety of positions from screenwriter and script consultant to line and consulting producer. For the past decade, she has designed and led dozens of exciting impact campaigns including A Crime on the Bayou, directed by Nancy Buirski, A Reckoning in Boston, directed by James Rutenbeck or Traces of the Trade: A Story from the Deep North, directed by Katrina Browne.

Marga has also worked with a variety of film festivals internationally. Since 2016, she is the outreach and engagement director for Double Exposure, a unique industry gathering that every October brings to DC the best investigative documentaries of the year along with a pitch forum and a wealth of opportunities for filmmakers.

Marga holds a master’s degree in Journalism and Media Studies from Complutense University of Madrid (Spain) where she worked in the film and television industries as a screenwriter and producer. Before relocating to the United States, Marga lived in Madrid, Spain, where she worked on national television, co-founded a successful production and communications agency, worked as a screenwriter and screenwriting teacher at a local film school, Metropolis. More info at twinseasmedia.com

speakers.name: Mohammad Al Abdallah
speakers.bio: Mohammad Al Abdallah is a Syrian human rights and democracy researcher and activist. He received a Bachelor’s of Law from the Lebanese University in 2007, and a Master’s of Public Policy from George Mason University in 2014. He previously worked as a research assistant for Human Rights Watch in Beirut from where he covered Syria. Al Abdallah is a former political prisoner who was imprisoned in Syria on two separate occasions for his work defending human rights and lobbying for political reform.

speakers.name: Mark Greenblatt
speakers.bio: Mark Greenblatt is the senior national investigative correspondent for the Scripps Washington Bureau and Newsy. His video, text and radio reports have earned three Peabody awards, the duPont-Columbia Award, the I.R.E. Medal, the Livingston Award, multiple national Edward R. Murrow Awards, and the national Emmy for investigative reporting, along with multiple regional Emmy awards. His reports have led to changes in laws at all levels of government, along with wholesale reforms of institutions. His investigative pieces for Scripps prompted Congress to close the military sex offender registration loophole and led to the felony indictment of a Veterans Administration hospital chief of staff, among other reforms. For Newsy, his “Case Cleared” series of reports revealed how dozens of police departments nationally mask the truth about how many rape investigations they really solve, clearing rape cases from their books with a little known tool called “exceptional clearance,” even when police leave the suspect on the streets with no arrest. Greenblatt was a co-lead on the investigation, which chronicled how some of those cleared suspects go on to find new victims. The report led to calls for change from within the Department of Justice. It also prompted the FBI to fast-track a process expected to reform the entire national uniform crime report to require all police agencies report more information about the outcomes of crime investigations. In Austin, the series prompted a state audit, which confirmed Austin police were inappropriately clearing rape cases. The reporting also prompted the Austin city council to unanimously pass a resolution directing a start to finish review of nearly 2,000 rape investigations over seven years. The third party review is slated to become one of the most ambitious reviews of police handling of rape investigations in American history. Mark regularly combines the use of databases and sources to unpack systemic flaws and issues of injustice. He volunteers as the treasurer for the D.C.- based Fund For Investigative Journalism and lives in Alexandria, Va., with his wife and daughter, where he roots for the Red Sox and brews his own beer.

speakers.name: Kelly Cole
speakers.bio:
Kelly Cole is a Lecturer in the English Department at Georgetown University. She teaches courses in Television History, Film Studies, and Advertising and serves on the faculty of the American Studies and Film and Media Studies Programs.

Cole has taught media studies at Middlebury College and in the Masters Program at the New School University. She holds a Ph.D. from the University of Wisconsin, Madison in Communication Arts. Her research focuses on media regulation and policy and issues of race and gender in the media.

speakers.name: Brad Forder
speakers.bio: Brad Forder is the Director of Programming for the Environmental Film Festival in the Nation’s Capital. He has worked as the director of photography for various documentary projects and has served as a videographer for the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. He holds a bachelor’s in Asian studies from Furman University and a master’s in international journalism from Cardiff University.

speakers.name: Kevin Hall
speakers.bio: Kevin Hall is the chief economics correspondent and a senior investigator at McClatchy Newspapers. He shared the 2017 Pulitzer Prize for Explanatory Reporting on the Panama Papers. He is also a past president of the Society of American Business Editors and Writers, the nation’s premier association for business journalists.

speakers.name: Chloe Gbai
speakers.bio:
Chloe Gbai is the Director for the IF/Then Shorts program. Through a competitive process, IF/Then Shorts identifies and supports original, standalone short documentaries by filmmakers working regionally and representing their communities. In an effort to discover and empower underrepresented voices, each pitch has a different regional focus. Beginning with an open call for submissions, IF/Then and a partner film festival select up to 6 filmmaking teams to present their projects at a live pitch competition at the film festival, before a jury of industry representatives. One filmmaker selected from each competition receives up to $25,000 in completion funding for their short film, year-round mentorship, and the opportunity to participate in the IF/Then distribution initiative.

Chloe joined IF/Then from American Documentary, where she was tapped by the 30-year-old PBS series to bring more short documentaries to its broadcast and streaming platforms. In 2018, she launched POV Shorts, which earned POV its third documentary short Oscar nomination, two News & Doc Emmy nominations and an IDA Awards nomination for Best Short Form Series. She has previously worked at Teen Vogue and Viacom as well as served on review panels and juries for the National Endowment for the Arts, Sheffield Doc/Fest, Austin Film Festival, IDA Awards, Black Public Media, Black Harvest Film Festival, and various other organizations. Her personal work centers around immigration, gender and race. She is a member of Brown Girls Doc Mafia, a member-in-residence of the Meerkat Media Collective, and a 2020 Impact Partners Producing Fellow.

Chloe will be facilitating the From IF/Then To The World: A Case Study On Multi-platform Distribution For Short Docs workshop.

speakers.name: Jill Wine-Banks
speakers.bio:
Jill Wine-Banks combines experience as a senior corporate executive and nonprofit CEO and COO with a successful legal career in government and private practice and service on corporate and civic boards. She began her career as an organized crime prosecutor at the U.S. Department of Justice in Washington, where, after just over four years, her trial capabilities and win record led to her selection as one of the three Assistant Watergate Special Prosecutors in the Watergate obstruction of justice trial against President Nixon’s top aides in which the President was named an unindicted co-conspirator. She was also a major player in the tapes hearing, cross examining Rose Mary Woods, President Nixon’s secretary, about the 18 ½ minute gap in a key White House recording.

Wine-Banks is a sought-after speaker for professional and business groups, universities and law schools. She is now an MSNBC Contributor and Legal Analyst. Before that she frequently appeared on other broadcast and cable channels and still appears on radio, PBS, several podcasts, and Australian and Canadian television. She has also written OpEds for the Chicago Tribune, Politico, and The Huffington Post.

She has been the recipient of many awards, including several from the United States Department of Justice and the highest civilian award given by the United States Department of the Army, as well as awards from the Girl Scouts, the YWCA, the Women’s Bar Association, and a Lifetime Achievement Award from Who’s Who in America. She also appears in other Who’s Who editions.

She has a B.S. in Communications from the University of Illinois Champaign-Urbana, a J.D. from Columbia University School of Law in New York City, and an Honorary Doctor of Law from Hood College.

speakers.name: Brandon Kramer
speakers.bio: Brandon Kramer is an award-winning documentary filmmaker and artistic director/co-founder of the DC-based production company Meridian Hill Pictures. he is the director of the feature documentary City of Trees, which played at the Full Frame Documentary Film Festival, was nationally broadcast on PBS’ America Reframed and is now streaming on Netflix and iTunes. He directed the Webby Award-winning documentary series The Messy Truth with Van Jones, released on Van Jones’ Facebook page and CNN.com just before the 2016 election to over 4 million viewers. He is the winner of the Best Director award at the 2016 Chesapeake Film Festival and Indie Capital Awards, received the Audience Choice Award at the 2015 American Conservation Film Festival and was a 2015 DC Commission on the Arts & Humanities Individual Arts Fellow. Since 2010, he has directed and produced over 30 short documentaries commissioned by government agencies and nonprofits including the AARP Foundation, the US Institute of Peace and the International Baccalaureate. Before starting Meridian Hill Pictures, he served as a staff teaching artist for the John F. Kennedy Center’s national media education program. Kramer holds a bachelor’s degree in film production and cultural anthropology from Boston University.

speakers.name: David Kaplan
speakers.bio:
David Kaplan has worked as an investigative journalist for more than 35 years, reported from two dozen countries and won or shared more than 25 awards. He has managed nonprofit newsrooms, investigative teams and numerous cross-border projects. During the 1980s and early 1990s, at the original Center for Investigative Reporting in San Francisco, he and his colleagues developed the model of a nonprofit investigative news enterprise. At its peak, CIR derived 40 percent of its income from commercial revenue, drawing from television news retainers, documentary production, publishing contracts and syndication. In 2008, Kaplan became editorial director of the Center for Public Integrity. At CPI, he rebuilt the newsroom’s editorial structure and data journalism unit, and revitalized what was then its global team, the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists. During his three years as ICIJ director, he tripled its funding, expanded its reach into 20 languages and oversaw internationally acclaimed investigations into the tobacco, asbestos, fishing and energy industries.

Kaplan is a four-time winner of the Investigative Reporters and Editors Award, including three medals, IRE’s highest honor. His work has also been honored four times by the Overseas Press Club. Until 2007 he worked as chief investigative correspondent for US News & World Report, then a two-million circulation newsweekly. Kaplan’s US News stories included exposés of racketeering by North Korean diplomats, Saudi funding of terrorist groups and the looting of Russia. His books include YAKUZA, published in 12 languages and widely considered the standard reference on the Japanese mafia. He has worked in media development for 20 years and has trained more than a thousand reporters worldwide in his investigative journalism workshops.

speakers.name: Mei Fong
speakers.bio: Pulitzer-prize winning journalist and author Mei Fong covered Asia as a Wall Street Journal correspondent. Her first book, on China’s one-child policy, won a non-fiction award by the American Society of Journalists and Authors, was chosen as one of the top non-fiction books of 2016 by Zocalo and Medium and is called “a searing, important, and eminently readable exploration of China’s one-child policy,” by Nick Kristof in the New York Review of Books. She is a fellow at DC think tank New America and listed in Foreign Policy magazine as a Top 50 influencer on US-China relations. Fong was born in Malaysia and holds a bachelor’s degree from the National University of Singapore and a master’s in international relations from Columbia University.

speakers.name: Dorothy Parvaz
speakers.bio:
Dorothy Parvaz is the Global Politics Reporter at ThinkProgess, covering U.S. foreign policy and all that it includes (diplomacy, security, trade, refugees and conflicts).

She previously worked at Al Jazeera English & America for nearly 7 years, focusing on migration, conflict, democracy and human rights in the MENA region and beyond. She has covered the refugee crisis in Iraq, Afghanistan, Greece and Italy and reported on the plight of Yazidi girls taken by ISIS, the turmoil in post-revolution Libya, and political upheaval in Egypt.

She previously worked at several daily newspapers in the United States, covering everything from culture to transportation policy.

Born in Iran, Parvaz was raised in Tehran, Dubai, and Vancouver, Canada, and has held fellowships and residencies at Harvard, Cambridge and the Rockefeller Foundation’s Bellagio Centre.

speakers.name: Wendy Benjaminson
speakers.bio:
Wendy Benjaminson has been a journalist, reporting and editing in Washington, DC, and Houston for more than 30 years. She is the managing editor for McClatchy’s Washington bureau. She joined McClatchy earlier this year after 12 years at The Associated Press, where she served as Texas News editor, national security editor and assistant bureau chief, and acting bureau chief. She was also a managing editor for government and politics at USA TODAY, and over 13 years, she worked in a number of positions at the Houston Chronicle, including politics editor and Metro editor to assistant managing editor for Sunday and special projects.

A 1983 graduate of the University of Maryland, Benjaminson has also covered Virginia state politics and government, Congress, the White House, trade issues and overseen coverage of the Pentagon, State Department and US policy in the Middle East, including Afghanistan, Iraq and Syria. Benjaminson has been nominated five times in six years for the Pulitzer Prize.

speakers.name: Tim Johnson
speakers.bio:
Tim Johnson currently covers cybersecurity as a national reporter for McClatchy’s Washington Bureau. He was part of a McClatchy team that shared a 2017 Pulitzer Prize for its work on the Panama Papers investigation that shone a light on the world of offshore companies. Previously, he served as bureau chief for McClatchy in Mexico City and in Beijing, roaming across Asia. In the 1990s, The Miami Herald posted him to Central America and the Andean region. In 1996, he was awarded the Maria Moors Cabot Prize by Columbia University for “courageous and valiant reporting” in Latin America. In earlier jobs, he served for UPI in Lima, Peru, and held a fellowship from the Inter American Press Association in Santiago, Chile.

Johnson was a Knight Journalism Fellow at Stanford University in 2000-2001. He is the author of Tragedy in Crimson: How the Dalai Lama Conquered the World but Lost the Battle with China (Nation Books), published in February 2011.

speakers.name: Kyra Darnton
speakers.bio: Kyra Darnton is the executive producer of Retro Report. She came to Retro Report from 60 Minutes, where she produced stories covering everything from the Mexican drug war to counterfeit prescription drugs to the cover up in the death of U.S. Ranger Pat Tillman. At 60 Minutes, her investigative reporting and storytelling won multiple awards, including a 2012 Peabody Award for a piece exposing fraud in cancer clinical trials. At Retro Report, she has overseen more than 150 short films with multiple distribution partners ranging from The New York Times to The New Yorker to PBS. Retro Report has won numerous awards including Emmy awards, Edward R. Murrow awards, Webby awards, and a 2018 Gerald Loeb award. Darnton has worked in journalism for 25 years.

speakers.name: Laura Blumenfeld
speakers.bio: Laura Blumenfeld is a Middle East analyst, a New York Times best-selling author, and a senior fellow at The Philip Merrill Center for Strategic Studies at Johns Hopkins School for Advanced International Studies. She previously served as a senior policy advisor on the State Department’s Israeli-Palestinian Negotiating Team. Blumenfeld was an award-winning reporter for The Washington Post for twenty years, covering the Middle East, national security, and presidential politics. She has been a senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund and a public policy fellow at The Wilson Center. She has written for The New Yorker, The New York Times Magazine, the Financial Times, and has appeared on CNN, FOX, MSNBC, BBC. She is the author of Revenge: A Story of Hope, a global study of revenge and reconciliation, translated into eight languages, optioned by HBO. Blumenfeld is a graduate of Harvard College and Columbia School of International and Public Affairs.

speakers.name: Frank Smyth
speakers.bio: Frank Smyth is the founder and CEO of Global Journalist Security (GJS), the leading U.S.-based hostile environments training firm. A social enterprise firm, GJS trains journalists and humanitarian professionals operating in high-risk environments around the world. GJS also helps subsidize training in collaboration with nonprofit groups for freelance journalists and activists.

speakers.name: Marcia Davis
speakers.bio: Marcia Davis is the news editor for The Marshall Project. She is responsible for helping to develop stories for the nonprofit, nonpartisan news organization. The Marshall Project seeks to sustain a sense of urgency about the U.S. criminal justice system. Before recently joining the staff, she spent more than 20 years at The Washington Post. Her jobs included working for metro, features and the national desk. Her last job was as an editor on The Washington Post Magazine. She is especially proud to have edited the magazine’s 2016 commemorative issue on the National Museum of African American History and Culture. Born in St. Louis, she also helped lead The Washington Post coverage of the fatal shooting of Michael Brown, the 18-year-old teenager killed by police. She also worked for Emerge magazine and the Minneapolis Star Tribune.

speakers.name: Poh Si Teng
speakers.bio:
Poh Si Teng is an Emmy-nominated director and senior commissioning producer for Witness, the flagship observational documentary strand of Al Jazeera English (International). She commissions documentaries and looks out for acquisitions and co-productions from the Americas for Witness.

She recently commissioned and senior produced Venezuela: Smuggling Dreams; Children of the FARC; Deportees Welcome: Between MS-13 and Call Centers; and A Cold War Family Reunion. (Venezuela: Smuggling Dreams is a finalist for the 2018 Rory Peck Current Affairs Award.)

Teng was previously a journalist for The New York Times, where she received an Emmy nomination for outstanding interview, a NPPA award, and a Society of Professional Journalists’ Deadline award for her documentary, Flirting With The Islamic State.

She was also part of the team that received a Public Service Reporting Award from the Scripps Howard Foundation for the Fatal Flaws investigation, which exposed widespread inattention to safety defects by automakers, suppliers and regulators. The investigation contributed to the recall of 60 million vehicles.

Prior to joining The Times, she was a freelance journalist and producer based in New Delhi, covering South Asia for Agence France-Presse. She was also previously a cameraperson for The Associated Press.

Born and raised in Penang, Malaysia, Teng is currently based in Washington, DC.

speakers.name: Patrick Radden Keefe
speakers.bio: Patrick Radden Keefe is a staff writer at The New Yorker magazine. He is the author of The Snakehead: An Epic Tale of the Chinatown Underworld and the American Dream, Chatter: Dispatches from the Secret World of Global Eavesdropping, and a new book, Say Nothing: A True Story of Murder and Memory in Northern Ireland, which will be published by Doubleday in early 2019. He received the National Magazine Award for Feature Writing in 2014, was a finalist for the National Magazine Award for Reporting in 2015 and 2016, and received an Emmy Award for executive producing the virtual reality film The People’s House.

speakers.name: Justine Gubar
speakers.bio:
Justine Gubar serves as Senior Editor for the Sunday Long Read Newsletter, curating the Long View section that identifies top videos and films of the week.

Until recently, Gubar was the Vice President of News Narratives for Fusion, the English-language cable network owned by Univision. In this role, she served as Executive Producer for the award winning investigative documentary series The Naked Truth. The series has been honored with multiple journalism awards including the RFK awards, NABJ, and a National Headliner Award. The first season of the series is now available on Netflix.

In 2015, she authored the book Fanaticus: Mischief and Madness in the Modern Sports Fan which was published by Rowman and Littlefield. The book is based on much of her experience as a producer for ESPN. At ESPN for two decades, she covered a wide range of off-the-field issues including performance enhancing drug use, domestic violence and homophobia in sports.

In 2011, she was honored with a Women in Cable Television (WICT) Signature Accolade award for Herstory: Ten Times Over, a documentary about basketball camps for girls in Nigeria. This project also received a NAMIC (National Association of Multi-Ethnicity in Communications) Vision award. For the academic year of 2006-7, she was awarded a John S. Knight Fellowship at Stanford University.

A graduate of Wesleyan University, Gubar is a native New Yorker.

speakers.name: Linnan Lin
speakers.bio:
[vc_row][vc_column][vc_column_text]Linnan Lin is a filmmaker and a jazz vocalist, and she loves working with 16mm film and a Bolex camera.

Linnan has received film recognition from festivals in the New England and New York areas for her film, How To Become Image Spam, an “experimental documentary” about the proliferation of imagery in modern day society.

She’s a recent graduate from Mount Holyoke College where she majored in film studies. Before joining Double Exposure, Linnan was living in China with her family while working on an independent film project about “Chinese Granny” dance culture.

Having just relocated to Washington, DC, Linnan is thrilled to be joining the Metropolitan Area film community.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row][vc_column][vc_btn title=”Contact Information” style=”custom” custom_background=”#99ff33″ custom_text=”#000000″ shape=”square” size=”lg” link=”url:mailto%3Alinnan%40dxfest.com|||”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row][vc_column][vc_column_text]linnan@dxfest.com[/vc_column_text][/vc_column][/vc_row]

speakers.name: Doyle McManus
speakers.bio:
Doyle McManus is a Washington columnist for the Los Angeles Times and director of the Journalism Program at Georgetown University. His column appears on the op-ed page of the Los Angeles Times and other newspapers nationwide. He has appeared frequently on PBS’ Washington Week, NPR and other broadcast media.

McManus has served as a police reporter in Los Angeles, a foreign correspondent in the Middle East and Europe, an investigative reporter in Washington and a White House correspondent. He was Washington bureau chief for the Los Angeles Times from 1996 to 2008.

He is a four-time winner of the National Press Club’s Edwin Hood Award for reporting on U.S. foreign policy, most recently for articles on the U.S. occupation of Iraq. He also won the American Academy of Diplomacy’s Arthur Ross Award for commentary on international affairs.

He is the coauthor of three books, including (with Jane Mayer) Landslide: The Unmaking of the President, named one of the notable books of 1988 by The New York Times.

speakers.name: Miasarah Lai
speakers.bio: Miasarah Lai is an independent documentary filmmaker and freelancer based in Chicago. From the Lower East Side, New York City, Lai’s Puerto Rican-Chinese heritage and diverse neighborhood shaped her global interests in visualizing alternative female and minority narratives. Her work has screened at film festivals including Athens Ethnofest, Human Rights Human Dignity International Film Festival, Wathann Film Festival, American Documentary Film Festival, Los Angeles Asian Pacific Film Festival, New Orleans Film Festival and Big Sky Film Festival. When she is not working on her own projects, Lai organizes two feminist collectives: Ethnocine, an ethnographic filmmaking collective, and Mezcla Media Collective, a hub for filmmakers of color in Chicago.

speakers.name: Mo’uth Freihat
speakers.bio: Mo’uth Freihat is an independent investigative journalist, co-founder and managing editor of Hashatagarabi.com, and co-founder and general manager of Tomatocartoon Magazine, with thirteen years reporting on the Arab world. He covered corruption and governance issues for Thomson Reuters Foundation and was managing editor of al Maqar.com, a major online news site in Jordan, for two years. A former financial reporter for Al Arab Al Youm, a Jordanian daily, Freihat also worked as a correspondent for several magazines on scholarly journals the politics and economy of the Gulf States. He has bachelor’s degree in international relations and strategic studies from Hashemite University in Jordan.

speakers.name: Melissa Beatriz
speakers.bio:
Melissa Beatriz is a documentary filmmaker, media educator, writer, and cultural worker based in Philadelphia. As an artist, she believes that visual images and film have the power to create social change in order to resist the injustices that immigrants, people of color, and marginalized groups face. Her media work focuses on advancing immigrant rights, education equality, and decarceration, as well as preserving folkloric arts and culture. Influenced by growing up in a bicultural Uruguayan-American familia, her projects are often bilingual.

Since 2010, she has been working with grassroots organizations, arts/cultural spaces, and film festivals throughout Philadelphia, while using a range of tools for community building and storytelling. Some of these collaborations include working with Scribe Video Center, BlackStar Film Festival, PHL Latino Film Festival, Reentry Think Tank, Media Mobilizing Project (MMP), and Taller Puertorriqueño.

Beatriz’s recent documentary film collaborations include Baobab Flowers (creative producer), When Life Gives You Lemons (director), and The Engine of My Life (co-director). She is currently directing a project that centers the stories of immigrant rights leaders in Philadelphia, in partnership with the #ShutDownBerks campaign. She was invited to participate in the Sundance Institute’s 2017 New Frontier Philadelphia Day Lab intensive and the Public VR Lab. Beatriz is a Double Exposure Scholar (2018) and an MMP Movement Media Fellow (2014). She is a recipient of the Leeway Foundation Window of Opportunity (2017) and Art & Change (2012) grants.

Beatriz is a member of the Brown Girls Doc Mafia (BGDM), a collective of women and non-binary filmmakers and industry representatives of color.

speakers.name: Ivan Angelovski
speakers.bio: Ivan Angelovski is an investigative reporter with 15+ years of experience. Originally from Belgrade, Serbia, he currently resides in Washington, DC and works as a freelance investigative journalist cooperating with several newsrooms in the Balkans.

speakers.name: Aisha Amin
speakers.bio: Aisha Amin is a NYC-based filmmaker and journalist. After graduating from Smith College with a degree in neuroscience, Amin developed an interest in non-fiction film and its relationship to human psychology. Her work focuses on issues surrounding Muslim-America identity, civil rights and criminal justice. Her past short films include Sonia and Incarcerating the Mentally Ill. Her past photo projects incorporate documentary with narration and poetry. Amin is also a freelance film critic and writer. Her work has been published in The Huffington Post, sister-hood magazine and Operation Condor. She is currently working as a programming fellow at American Documentary’s POV, helping to launch the short film program slate.

speakers.name: Lauren Durr
speakers.bio:
Lauren Durr is a native of Baton Rouge, Louisiana, and discovered a love for classic films and television at an early age. She pursued a degree at the Communications School of Elon University in North Carolina and graduated with a Bachelor of Arts in 2005. She began her career working as an editor at the CBS station, WRAL, in Raleigh, North Carolina. She would spend the next five years in Raleigh working in both news and a local production company, Drawbridge Media, specializing in producing and editing corporate video and reality television.  

Durr moved to New York in 2010 to pursue reality television editing. To date she has edited countless shows airing on networks including TLC, A&E, Discovery, HGTV, CNBC, and the Up Network. She specializes in character-driven shows that focus on relationships among many characters. In 2016, Durr directed and edited 1000 Year Flood, a feature investigative documentary focusing on the devastation of and recovery from Louisiana’s Great Flood. She currently lives in Los Angeles and continues to pursue a career in television.

speakers.name: Daniyar Kosnazarov
speakers.bio: Daniyar Kosnazarov’s research interests include youth, social media, and popular culture. As a visiting fellow at The George Washington University, his research focuses on the values and higher education expectations of Kazakhstan’s Generation Z. Kosnazarov is also the Editor-in-Chief of Steppe, an independent digital media outlet in Kazakhstan covering technology, entrepreneurship, education, leisure, and art. He is experienced working for both the government and private think tanks of Kazakhstan, and previously worked as Chair of the Department of Strategic Analysis at Narxoz University, evaluating strategy implementation. He previously was awarded an Master of Arts in International Relations and Regional Studies from Tsukuba University in Japan, and a Bachelor of Arts in International Relations from Selcuk University in Turkey.

speakers.name: Micah Garen
speakers.bio:
Micah Garen is an award-winning documentary filmmaker and journalist who has worked in conflict and post-conflict zones for the past 15 years directing over two dozen short and features films. Most recently, he has directed five films for Al Jazeera English, one of which, Identity & Exile, won a Golden Nymph for Best News Documentary at the Monte Carlo Television Festival in 2014. His work has been published in Al Jazeera English, The New York Times, The New York Times Magazine, The Intercept, Vanity Fair, Newsweek and the Financial Times, among others.  

In 2004, Garen and his interpreter Amir were kidnapped while filming in Iraq. They were held for ten days before being released. Their story is chronicled in the dual-memoir, with Marie-Hélène Carleton, American Hostage, published by Simon & Schuster in 2005. The memoir received starred reviews on both Kirkus and Publisher’s Weekly. Garen got his start filming in Iraq in 2003 as part of Michael Moore’s award-winning Fahrenheit 911. 

Garen has been awarded artist fellowships at the MacDowell Colony and the Ucross Foundation and was selected to participate in the inaugural Film Independent Documentary Lab in LA and the IFP Documentary Film Lab. He co-founded Four Corners Media and ScreeningRoom with his partner Marie-Hélène Carleton.

speakers.name: Marie-Hélène Carleton
speakers.bio:
Marie-Hélène Carleton is an award-winning documentary filmmaker. Most recently, she has directed five documentaries for Al Jazeera English, one of which, Identity & Exile, won Best News Documentary at the Monte Carlo Festival of Television and Film in 2014.

Her recent short film about the refugee crisis, Light on the Sea, launched in March on Vanity Fair and The Scene. Her short film about the Egyptian uprisings in Tahrir Square of 2011, Four Women, One Revolution, won the Women and Girls Matter award for Media that Matters. Her film work has appeared on Al Jazeera English, Vanity Fair, BBC America, The New York Times, the Financial Times, HDNet’s World Report and Granta Magazine, among others.

She is a member of Film Fatales and has been awarded artist fellowships at the MacDowell Colony and the Ucross Foundation. She was selected to participate in the inaugural Film Independent Documentary Lab in LA and the IFP Documentary Film Lab.  Carleton co-founded Four Corners Media and ScreeningRoom with her partner Micah Garen.

speakers.name: Ashley Bloom Kenny
speakers.bio: Ashley Bloom Kenny is a senior producer for Atlantic Studios where she oversees the production of The Atlantic’s original documentaries, series and animations. Prior to joining The Atlantic, Kenny spent three years as a series producer for Al Jazeera America’s Documentary Unit commissioning and managing original documentary series for the premier feature slot on Sunday nights. Before joining Al Jazeera, Kenny spent eight years at National Geographic developing, directing and producing dozens of original documentary specials and series worldwide.

speakers.name: Aldo E. Mendoza-Guerra
speakers.bio:
Aldo E. Mendoza-Guerra is a Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipient who immigrated to the U.S. in 2000 unlawfully with his mother and father at the age of four. His family fled from an economically devastated country in hopes for a better life. Mendoza-Guerra grew up in Athens, Ga., and attends the University of North Georgia, where he is working on a political science degree.

Mendoza-Guerra has been an advocate for rights of the undocumented since 2010. He belongs to multiple organizations that advocate for undocumented student and undocumented rights. He has fought to lift the ban on undocumented immigrants from attending the top five universities in Georgia. The ban was started in 2010 by Georgia’s Board of Regents and has been reduced to the  top three universities in Georgia.

speakers.name: Rachel de Leon
speakers.bio: Rachel de Leon is a video producer for Reveal. She produces news segments and documentaries based on investigations in the Reveal newsroom. De Leon has worked for more than 10 years as a videographer and producer. Throughout 2017, she was the coordinating producer for Glassbreaker Films – an initiative from The Center for Investigative Reporting to support female filmmakers – helping to produce five half-hour documentaries for national and festival distribution, and more than 20 online mini-documentaries. In 2016, she won two Emmys for her work on the web series “The Dead Unknown” and the PBS NewsHour segment “Deadly Oil Fields.” In 2014, she completed her first short documentary, “Cab City,” for her master’s thesis in the documentary program at the U.C. Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism. De Leon is based in Reveal’s Emeryville, Calif., office.

speakers.name: Anabelle Rojas
speakers.bio: Anabelle Rojas is the production manager in charge for all programming strands of Al Jazeera English in Washington, DC. She spent the earlier part of her career of more than 10 years in a variety of roles within the Finance department of the Al Jazeera Media Network. She provided financial support to programs management by working closely with the production teams of long- form documentaries, children’s programming and digital productions to ensure all projects stayed within budget. She also collaborated with the Director of Business Affairs by ensuring transparent and efficient contracting of independent production companies, and freelance contractors working on programs projects. In her current position, she has oversight of all operational and financial matters for in-house and commission productions as well as discussion programs. Rojas partners with the editorial management to ensure the smooth operations from pre-production, budget developing and monitoring and cost reporting to successful delivery of all Al Jazeera English productions out of Washington, DC.

speakers.name: Lea Trusty
speakers.bio:
Lea Trusty is a Program Associate on the Public Square team at Democracy Fund, a private foundation working to ensure that our political system is able to withstand new challenges and deliver on its promise to the American people. 

Lea supports the Engaged Journalism strategy in its mission to invest in innovations and institutions that focus on creating audience-centered, inclusive, and trusted newsrooms that reflect the diversity of their communities. She leads their portfolio centered on diversity, equity, and inclusion in journalism. Current grantees include organizations like the Maynard Institute, Ida B. Wells Society, and Take the Lead.

Lea joined Democracy Fund in summer 2017. Prior to joining the team, Lea was a Newman’s Own Foundation Fellow, a program for recent graduates interested in philanthropy and social impact. She was placed at WSHU Public Radio, an NPR affiliate in Connecticut. She covered a wide breadth of stories, from minority teacher recruitment to the first family suing ICE for detention center abuses.

Lea is currently a member of the EPIP DC steering committee. She graduated magna cum laude from Princeton University, where she studied politics and Latin America.

Lea will be moderating the In the Crosshairs: Doxxing, Trolling and the Weaponization of Social Media panel.

speakers.name: Sheila Leddy
speakers.bio: Sheila Leddy is the Executive Director of the Fledgling Fund, a small private foundation driven by the belief that powerful visual stories can spur action around issues that affect the most vulnerable. Through its grant programs, labs and special initiatives it explores, supports, and deepens the role of documentary film and other forms of visual storytelling in larger social change efforts. Leddy has worked with the fund since its founding, where she has been integral to the development of the organization’s overall strategy, collaborating with President and Founder Diana Barrett and the board of directors. She continues to play a leadership role shaping Fledgling’s strategy, operations, grantmaking and other initiatives.

speakers.name: Margaret Mishi Ebrahim
speakers.bio: Mishi Ebrahim (she/her) is the senior director of programming and development at PBS. She is a journalist, producer and media executive who creates, identifies, develops and executive produces unscripted series, documentaries and timely news-oriented specials integrating exceptional journalism with creative storytelling. At PBS, she oversees the news and current affairs content portfolio, including FRONTLINE and NewsHour, as well as commissions and acquires nonfiction films and series across platforms. Ebrahim has worked at some of the most successful media organizations like CBS News 60 Minutes, National Geographic, ABC News and the Investigative Reporting Workshop at American University. She’s a member of the board of directors for 100 Reporters, the parent organization of the DX Film Festival.

speakers.name: Laila Al-Arian
speakers.bio:
Laila Al-Arian is a Washington, D.C. based journalist and the executive producer of FAULT LINES, an award-winning current affairs program on Al Jazeera English. She has produced documentaries on subjects ranging from the Trump administration’s Muslim ban to the impact of the heroin epidemic on children, and an investigation into factory conditions producing garments for Walmart and Gap in Bangladesh. For her work, she has been honored with two News and Documentary Emmys, a Peabody Award, a Robert F. Kennedy Award in journalism, Overseas Press Club Award, National Headliner Award, and has been nominated for eight News and Documentary Emmys.

Prior to joining FAULT LINES, Laila worked for Al Jazeera English for four years, covering everything from Guantanamo Bay’s youngest detainee to the resettlement of Iraqi refugees in the U.S. She received a B.A. in English Literature from Georgetown University and an M.S. from Columbia’s Graduate School of Journalism. Her work has appeared in The Nation, Salon, The Independent, and other publications, and she is co-author of the book Collateral Damage: America’s War Against Iraqi Civilians.

Laila will be facilitating the Fact-Checking In The Age Of Misinformation workshop and taking meetings for DX Access.

speakers.name: Luisa Conlon
speakers.bio: Luisa Conlon is a documentary director and cinematographer based in Los Angeles. Her work has been published in The New York Times Op-Docs, The Atlantic, VICE, PBS NewsHour, and NPR. Her award-winning short documentary We Became Fragments was published by The New York Times Op-Docs with support from the Pulitzer Center on Crisis Reporting, the Tribeca Film Institute, and the Berkeley Film Foundation. Conlon received her Masters in Journalism from UC Berkeley’s Graduate School of Journalism.

speakers.name: Lance Kramer
speakers.bio: Lance Kramer is an award-winning documentary filmmaker and co-founder of the DC-based production company Meridian Hill Pictures. He produced the feature-length documentary City of Trees (Official Selection 2016 Full Frame Documentary Film Festival, National Broadcast on the PBS series America Reframed, released on Netflix in May 2017) and the Webby Award-winning documentary series The Messy Truth With Van Jones, released on Van’s Facebook page and CNN.com to more than 4 million viewers. In 2014, Kramer received the DC Mayor’s Arts Award from the DC Commission on the Arts and Humanities, the highest honor bestowed upon working artists in the city. He has served two terms as Board Member of Docs in Progress, and was a DC Commission on the Arts & Humanities Individual Arts Fellow in 2015. In 2017, he was selected to the 2017 Impact Partners Documentary Producers Fellowship cohort and in 2018 he was a fellow at the Sundance Creative Producers Summit. Kramer holds a bachelor’s degree in history and film from Dartmouth College.

speakers.name: Joanne Lawler
speakers.bio:
Joanne Lawler is responsible, with Anabelle Rojas, for production management of the Documentary and Discussion Program strands in Washington, DC. She ensures smooth operation from pre-production through delivery within allocated budgets, and is responsible for the management of the Programming internship and fellowship programs. Lawler has performed a variety of roles over the past 25 years in the television broadcast industry: administrator/coordinator for AJE Technical Operations, managing contracts and budgets for AJE in the Americas; station relations representative for DeShields Associates, providing marketing and support for public television programs; and video editor, highlights including award winning pieces for the Eye on America series, CBS Evening News, ABC World News Tonight, Nightline and 20/20 as well as independent documentary and advocacy films.

At Double Exposure, Joanne will hear pitches from filmmakers whose completed film is of global interest and would generate significant online discussion about the film and the deeper issues important to AJE’s online community.

speakers.name: Daniel Grinberg
speakers.bio: Daniel Grinberg is the Postdoctoral Fellow for the Annenberg School for Communication’s Center for Media at Risk at the University of Pennsylvania. His research focuses on issues related to documentary film, government documents and censorship, war and security media, and surveillance. His writing on documentary media has appeared in journals such as Studies in Documentary Film; Media, War & Conflict; Jump Cut; and the Journal of War and Culture Studies, and is forthcoming in Journal of Cinema and Media Studies and Media, Culture & Society. He is currently working on his first book, Partial Disclosures: Documentary Media and the Freedom of Information Act.

speakers.name: Joel Stonington
speakers.bio:
Joel Stonington has worked in journalism for more than a decade, writing about energy, crime, politics and other topics. He has previously reported for The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, Los Angeles Times, The Guardian, New York Magazine, Bloomberg Businessweek, Der Spiegel, MSNBC and ABC News. Stonington has received fellowships and funding to support reporting from the Kiplinger Program in Public Affairs Journalism, Humboldt Foundation and Carnegie Corporation.

Joel will be taking meetings for DX ACCESS / PITCH.

speakers.name: Melissa Houghton
speakers.bio: Melissa J. Houghton joined Women in Film & Video (WIFV) as Executive Director in August 2005. Since that time, membership has grown to more than 1,000 media professionals; program provision now averages 70 professional development offerings per year along with the Image Makers program for high school students and the Kids World Film Festival for 5th graders. Houghton has served on the boards of the DC Architectural Foundation, DC Film Alliance, and Wide Angle Youth Media. She is currently a member of the WETA Community Council, the FAVS Advisory Board at George Mason University and the Advisory Board for The Actors’ Center.

speakers.name: Adam Segal
speakers.bio:
[vc_row][vc_column][vc_column_text]Adam J. Segal is a film, television, and issues publicist based in the New York region. He founded The 2050 Group – Publicity, a full-service publicity and marketing agency, in 2006. The agency’s work is often focused on film, television, and digital projects that are at the intersection of entertainment and issues (whether they are political, social, or cultural and whether they are domestic or international).

In 2018 alone, agency clients received 13 national Emmy Award nominations. And in just the past five years, agency clients received at least 66 national Emmy Award nominations and nearly 150 industry film, television, and social impact awards nominations overall.

The 2050 Group – Publicity has been one of the nation’s leading entertainment and issues PR agencies offering full-service services to clients including Oscar nominated documentaries Edith + Eddie, Knife Skills, Joe’s Violin, 4.1 Miles, plus POV‘s Last Men in Aleppo, Miss Sharon Jones!, Hooligan Sparrow, The Work, Rumble: The Indians Who Rocked the World, The Waiting Room, Virunga, and many more.

The agency has handled publicity for numerous film festivals including Double Exposure Investigative Film Festival & Symposium, Traverse City Film Festival, Maryland Film Festival, and the Full Frame Documentary Film Festival.

Segal has been a speaker at numerous film industry events including the International Documentary Association’s Doc-U series, DOC NYC Pro conference, and the Hot Docs Canadian International Documentary Festival.

While working in the PR field, Segal served on the faculties of graduate-level communications programs at Johns Hopkins University and Georgetown University for nearly a decade. He is a graduate of Johns Hopkins University and The George Washington University.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row][vc_column][vc_btn title=”Contact Information” style=”custom” custom_background=”#99ff33″ custom_text=”#000000″ shape=”square” size=”lg” link=”url:mailto%3Aadam%40the2050group.com|||”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row][vc_column][vc_empty_space height=”20px”][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row][vc_column][vc_column_text]adam@the2050group.com[/vc_column_text][/vc_column][/vc_row]

speakers.name: Vishal Solanki
speakers.bio: Vishal Solanki holds a Bachelor of Fine Arts in Applied Art and honors in Film Directing and Cinematography from the Los Angeles Film School. For the last 12 years, he has been working as a full-time filmmaker in Los Angeles. His recent documentary feature Caffeinated premiered at the Santa Barbara International Film Festival in 2015 and subsequently released by Amazon Prime. Cora, a short drama he photographed, premiered at the 2016 Cannes Film Festival. Recent credits include cinematography for The Advocates which premieres at LA Film Festival 2018 followed by a theatrical release, cinematography for a documentary about child sex trafficking in America directed by PBS fellow Joanna Friedman, and cinematography for an online refugees’ archive called Stories of Syria. His cinematography work on Go Public, an award-winning documentary series, was featured on PBS, and he has done cinematography for PSAs of Sesame Street for HBO and PBS. Solanki is an associate of UC Berkeley’s IRP workshop; his scholarship was funded by the MacArthur Foundation and Knight Foundation. In 2018, he received a grant from Center for Cultural Innovation to attend the Getting Real 2018 conference organized by IDA. He is currently nominated to the FRONTLINE/Firelight fellowship for his investigative reporting documentary titled About Time. Solanki volunteers for the California Coalition for Women Prisoners and the International Documentary Association, and he is a guest speaker at the Dodge College of Art and Media at Chapman University for documentary production. In 2012, he started Evoke Mediaworks to empower communities through media.

speakers.name: Chris Renteria
speakers.bio:
Chris Renteria has produced and directed films focusing on the challenges, socially and environmentally, within the Southwest and Midwest regions. His work continues to focus on shining a light on a vibrant youth and documenting the voice of St. Louis future leaders. Magnolia Pictures’ Whose Streets? by Sabaah Folayan is Renteria’s first foray as a producer into feature-length documentary. The film premiered at the Sundance Film Festival in 2017. His work has been featured by Paramount Networks, CNN, Hearst TV, The Food Network, and PBS and published by numerous websites. He has held solo and group exhibitions across the country.

Renteria is co-­founder and creative producer for The St. Louis Photo Authority, a non­profit organization dedicated to promoting the visual arts and community engagement by training children and adults in storytelling with the mediums of photography and video.

speakers.name: Diane Quon
speakers.bio: Diane Quon is an Academy Award-nominated producer who worked as a marketing executive at NBC and at Paramount Pictures before moving back to her hometown of Chicago. Diane is producing the Kartemquin Films documentaries: Oscar and Emmy nominated, Peabody and Sundance award-winning film, Minding the Gap directed by Bing Liu; For the Left Hand along with Chicago Tribune arts critic Howard Reich, and co-directed by Leslie Simmer and Gordon Quinn; and The Dilemma of Desire with Peabody Award-winning director Maria Finitzo (SXSW 2020). She is also producing the documentary, Untitled Sam Project, directed by Nadav Kurtz and executive produced by Public Record; and Wuhan Wuhan directed by Yung Chang for Starlight Entertainment (Crazy Rich Asians). She is also developing a fiction film based on The New York Times best-selling book, Hotel on the Corner of Bitter and Sweet. She is an AMPAS member, a recipient of the 2020 Cinereach Producer Award, and is a Sundance Creative Producing Fellow,  an IFP Cannes Producer Fellow and a  Film Independent Fellow.

speakers.name: Bryan Pollard
speakers.bio:
Bryan Pollard is the Director of Programs and Strategic Partnerships at the Native American Journalists Association. Pollard is currently pursuing a master’s degree in journalism with an emphasis on documentary filmmaking. His first film, A Shelter First, about the homelessness crisis in Northwest Arkansas, is set for release this fall. He is a board member for High Country News, a nonprofit environmental and land use news magazine based in Colorado, and is a member of the Leadership Team for the Journalism Mentorship Collaborative sponsored by the Online News Association.

Prior to joining NAJA, he was the executive editor of the Cherokee Phoenix, the tribal news organization for the Cherokee Nation based in Tahlequah, Oklahoma. The Phoenix was the first Native American newspaper originally published in 1828. Pollard is also a founder of Street Roots, a nonprofit newspaper focused on issues of concern to the homeless and low-income citizens of Portland, Oregon.

Pollard has been a certified high school journalism teacher and taught at Sequoyah High School, an Indian boarding school in Tahlequah. He has served as a mentor for numerous journalism workshops including the Oklahoma Institute for Diversity in Journalism, the Society of Professional Journalists Working Press, the UNITY News and the NAJA Student Projects and Project Phoenix.

speakers.name: George Frampton
speakers.bio: George Frampton served as an Assistant Special Prosecutor on the Watergate Special Prosecution Force, US Department of Justice, from 1973 to 1975, where he worked on the grand jury investigation and trial of President Nixon’s top aides in the Watergate cover-up. He graduated from Yale College with a Bachelor of Arts in Physics, the London School of Economics with a M.Sc. Economics, with Distinction, in Advanced Economic Theory, and Harvard Law School where he was Treasurer (Managing Editor) of the Harvard Law Review.

speakers.name: Richard Ben-Veniste
speakers.bio:
Richard Ben-Veniste is a highly respected litigator who focuses on complex civil litigation and white collar criminal cases. He also advises organizations and individuals involved in congressional investigations across a broad range of complex and sensitive areas.

Ben-Veniste first achieved national prominence during the mid-1970s, when he served as one of the lead prosecutors on the Watergate Special Prosecution Force. Recognized as both a knowledgeable and experienced counselor and as a skilled and accomplished trial lawyer, he has been a key figure in some of the nation’s most significant governmental activities at the intersection of law and politics. Most recently, Ben-Veniste agreed to serve as a legal analyst for CNN.

speakers.name: Sarah Katz
speakers.bio: Sarah Katz has worked in television and multimedia as a producer, associate producer and researcher for more than seventeen years. In fall of 2018 she will lead eight journalists from South and Central Asia to Washington, DC, California, and Hawaii on a tour covering U.S. Indo-Pacific Strategy in light of China’s One Belt, One Road initiative. She routinely produces news stories about U.S. policy with foreign journalists as part of the Department of State’s Media Co-Op program. An upcoming documentary produced with Pakistani journalists will tell the story of Muslim communities in America. In May, Katz joined Marginal Revolution University, an economic policy center at George Mason University that produces educational videos. She is producing a historical documentary film about Washington, DC city politics with director Aimee Dixon. Katz has produced over one hundred and fifty-six half-hours of educational content for The Great Courses and has credits on over forty documentaries for the History Channel, National Geographic Television, Biography, Planet Green, and Investigation Discovery. She is a New Media Council member of the Producers Guild of America and a former Docs In Progress board member. At Docs In Progress she launched the Documentary Inspiration Awards celebrating the work of Marshall Curry and Matthew Hamachek. She received a Master of Fine Arts in Film from American University in 2009 for which she received the Guy P. Gannett journalism scholarship from the Maine Community Foundation. She has an undergraduate degree in French literature and spent a year volunteering in Zimbabwe.

speakers.name: Dez Hernandez
speakers.bio:
Dez Hernandez is passionate about pursuing truth and telling the untold, unknown, and misunderstood stories. Throughout his career, he has traveled the country extensively, gaining a unique perspective on the nation’s most important and divisive issues.

Hernandez’s most recent project is The Service Gap, a docu-series that explores alternate opportunities for American high school graduates–and why those needs exist in the first place. He was recently selected as a Latino Lens Incubator finalist by the National Association of Latino Independent Producers (NALIP). Hernandez has over a decade of experience with various mediums and productions, from HBO’s Luck and NBC’s American Ninja Warrior to PBS’ Veterans Coming Home digital series. He also served as a producer for the IUCN’s World Conservation Congress 2016 in Hawaii and his documentary, Baloeiros, shot in Brazil over a 6-year period, has a follow-up in the works. As a casting, development, story, field and line producer, he has created content for Animal Planet, TLC, Univision, A&E, WEtv, TRUtv and more. He is currently working on a slate of documentary and scripted projects, in addition to exploring new content opportunities in the technology and communications sectors.

speakers.name: Jarrad Henderson
speakers.bio: Jarrad Henderson is an Emmy-award winning video producer, award-winning visual journalist and filmmaker, who is respected for working strategically and efficiently with creative teams or independently in a deadline driven environments. An excellent student and teacher, Henderson is a 2018 Fellow with the Donald W. Reynolds Journalism Institute and helps others pursue their dreams of becoming visual storytellers through his roles as an Adjunct Professor at Georgetown University’s School of Continuing Studies and as the Chair of the National Association of Black Journalists – Visual Task Force. When he’s not sharing stories, Henderson enjoys spending time with his family, speaking and hitting the roller skating rink. His work reflects that harmonious human relationships are the keys to success.

sessions.title: Roundtable: Creating a New Impact Pipeline
sessions.description: Invite-only: This private industry session explores why documentaries can fill festival houses, then disappear. For most films, there’s no clear path to the local audiences who’d care most, and for most newsrooms and community organizations, no easy way to host a screening that sparks a real conversation. This facilitated, two-hour roundtable brings filmmakers, journalists, funders, and impact producers into one room to work on that gap together. It isn’t a panel or a pitch. Participants will compare notes on what’s gotten in the way, what has worked, and what would make bringing films to communities worthwhile for everyone involved. What comes out of the conversation will help shape what happens to documentaries after the festival circuit ends.
sessions.venue: Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg Center, 4th Floor Link Room
sessions.page_title: Roundtable: Creating a New Impact Pipeline

sessions.title: Roundtable: The Internet Archive and Documentary Film
sessions.description: Invite-only: This private industry session explores where a documentary lives once the festival run, the streaming deal, and the distributor’s interest are over? For many films, the answer is a hard drive, a platform that may change its terms, or nowhere at all. The Internet Archive wants to expand its role as a lasting home for documentary film, a nonprofit library where films can be preserved and freely accessed, independent of any one platform’s business decisions or shifting political and commercial pressures. In a conversation moderated by Kathleen Lingo, Mark Graham, Director of the Wayback Machine, will explain how the Archive works and what it could offer filmmakers. Then she’ll open the floor to members of the filmmaking community to hear what they need, what keeps them up at night, what’s on their wish list. This is a working conversation, not a pitch. Filmmakers and other stakeholders who bring questions, concerns, and ideas will help shape what the Archive builds.
sessions.venue: Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg Center, 4th Floor Link Room
sessions.page_title: Roundtable: The Internet Archive and Documentary Film

sessions.title: Arbiter: Uncovering the Digital Networks Gaming Your Brain
sessions.description:
The average person spends two hours a day browsing the social internet, consuming information that influences their decisions on everything from voting to healthcare to how they spend their money, and more. But which narratives might be influenced by hidden networks echoing claims in a coordinated manner, with the goal of dominating your feed? How can we uncover messaging that targets certain demographic groups to polarize them?

This session provides exclusive access to Arbiter, a private platform developed to investigate digital deception campaigns. The platform exposes the networks that shape your feed before it shapes your views. It provides a real-time solution to the question “How do you audit the digital information you are consuming before it shapes the lens through which you view the world?”

Arbiter has received signups from 150+ newsrooms and civil society orgs. in 40+ countries and was recently featured in a Nieman Journalism Lab cover story. At this hands-on workshop, Arbiter’s creator will run a digital investigation exclusive to each attendee, with free access for the duration of the session and shortly after. You will learn to create a digital investigation of your choosing into issues that are top of your mind, so that you can uncover the networks of accounts shaping the conversation across major social platforms, in under 45 minutes.
sessions.venue: Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg Center
sessions.page_title: Arbiter: Uncovering the Digital Networks Gaming Your Brain

sessions.title: DX Academy Masterclass:  The Making of The Oligarch and the Art Dealer and Rescue, with Andreas Dalsgaard
sessions.description:
How do you build an investigative film when neither side will give you the full story, and one of them won’t even meet you in person? And how do you tell a story whose subjects have almost no power at all, when filming could put them at greater risk?

Andreas Dalsgaard has faced both questions. As director of The Oligarch and the Art Dealer, Double Exposure’s Opening Night selection, he spent years unraveling a $2 billion art fraud dispute between a secretive Russian oligarch and the Swiss art dealer he accused of betrayal. The film parts the curtain on a borderless “Moneyland,” where fortunes move in secret beyond the reach of tax collectors and law enforcement. Along the way, it unearths masterpieces by Klimt, Gauguin, Van Gogh, Chagall and Leonardo da Vinci, that otherwise remain locked away in “freeport” vaults seen by almost no one.

As a producer of Sine Plambech’s Rescue, also screening at Double Exposure, Dalsgaard helped bring to the screen a story from the opposite end of the scale of power: a Yemeni family separated at sea during a rescue in the Mediterranean, and their desperate quest for safety.

In this session designed for students, Dalsgaard draws on both films to walk through the craft of investigative documentary: working where access is unequal and sources have every reason to lie; protecting vulnerable subjects while holding powerful ones to account; and leaving audiences room to weigh competing versions of the truth for themselves. It’s a real-world case study for anyone studying journalism, documentary or media production, and a rare chance to go behind the scenes of two of this year’s festival films.

sessions.title: The People’s Archive: What’s In It, How to Use It
sessions.description:
A conversation on the vast public record housed right here in Washington — historical photographs, civic documents, and primary sources anyone can access, often for free — and what it actually takes to turn an archive into a film. Lisa Warwick, the DC Public Library’s People’s Archivist, is joined by Marisa Fox, director of Double Exposure’s Closing Night film, My Underground Mother, and Bonnie Rowan, the archival researcher who helped unearth some of the buried records at the heart of Fox’s film. Come learn what’s actually in the archive, how to start using it for your own research, family history, or storytelling, and what it looks like when that research becomes a documentary. Moderated by filmmaker Doug Block, founder and co-host of The D-Word.

RSVP A FREE TICKET
sessions.venue: Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library
sessions.page_title: The People’s Archive: What’s In It, How to Use It

sessions.title: HOW TO KNOW WHAT’S REAL
sessions.description:
This workshop teaches practical, everyday habits for checking whether what you’re looking at is what it claims to be: how to trace where an image or video actually came from, what warning signs suggest manipulation, and what questions to ask before you share something or believe it. Bring your phone. Bring your skepticism. Leave with tools you’ll actually use.

BUY A STANDALONE TICKET
sessions.venue: The Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg Center

sessions.title: Restoring Reality: A Wayback Machine Deep Dive
sessions.description:
The Wayback Machine holds hundreds of billions of archived web pages — but knowing it exists and knowing how to actually find what you’re looking for are two different skills. This hands-on workshop, led by the Wayback Machine’s own director, walks participants through the practical mechanics of searching the archive: how to locate a deleted government page, track how a public statement changed over time, and verify that a record once existed even after it’s gone from the live web.

What you’ll leave with: the practical ability to find internet records yourself.

RSVP A FREE TICKET
sessions.venue: Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library
sessions.page_title: Restoring Reality: A Wayback Machine Deep Dive

sessions.title: Cast Out and Speaking Up
sessions.description:
Over the last two years, thousands of federal employees have been summarily dismissed. Some were forced out for political reasons, others as part of sweeping reductions that have gutted agencies responsible for public health, environmental protection, scientific research, foreign aid and national security. Private-sector workers who speak up about harm to the public face a parallel threat from Non-Disclosure Agreements, which the administration would like to impose as a new condition of federal employment. Some chose to speak when silence would have been safer. Their accounts, and the legal and personal costs they have borne, illuminate what is being lost inside government and industry alike, and what it takes to go on the record about it.

This session features whistleblowers and former employees, from federal agencies and the private sector, and the journalists and filmmakers who tell their stories. It is not a partisan panel: it is a reckoning with what accountability looks like from the inside, and what happens to those who exercise it.

BUY A STANDALONE TICKET
sessions.venue: The Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg Center

sessions.title: Faked, Erased, Distorted: Does the Record Matter?
sessions.description:
You’ve seen the footage. You’ve watched the clip. And at some point in the last few years, you’ve probably stopped and asked: is this even real?

That question used to belong to archivists and forensic experts. Now it belongs to everyone. AI has made it easier to generate, alter, or strip context from images and video, while disinformation campaigns and propaganda operations — run by governments and non-state actors alike — work to shape what the public sees and believes. At the same time, the record faces pressure from other directions: government agencies have removed or altered thousands of public datasets and webpages over the past year, and platforms have deleted or restricted access to years of public archives, from Twitter’s historical record to community forums that vanish when a company changes policy.

This session brings together people working to preserve and authenticate the record on every front: the Archival Producers Alliance, which helps documentary filmmakers verify the integrity of archival material; the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine, which has preserved more than 1 trillion web pages; and SimPPL, which is using AI to identify what’s influencing you faster than platforms and institutions. Together, they’ll take up the question at the center of it all: how do you keep a public record trustworthy when the tools to fake it, and the incentives to do so, are everywhere?

BUY A STANDALONE TICKET
sessions.venue: The Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg Center
sessions.page_title: Faked, Erased, Distorted: Does the Record Matter?

sessions.title: Your City Your Story
sessions.description:
What happens when a community stops waiting on institutions and does accountability’s work itself? In Los Angeles, the gay community banded together to investigate a cold case murder and push it toward resolution — the subject of Rachel Mason’s new film My Brother’s Killer. It’s happening nationwide as legacy news organizations scale back and new local news outlets emerge: Chicago-based City Bureau trains community members to cover public meetings; Outlier Media in Detroit involved citizens in connecting residents to money the county owed them after selling their homes at auction. Other news platforms train citizens in filing FOIA requests, with OpenAI even providing a generator to automate the process. This session is about building a record where none exists — tools for everyone, and the networks to use them safely.

BUY A STANDALONE TICKET
sessions.venue: The Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg Center

sessions.title: Visual Investigation Breakdown: How Evident revealed dangers of ‘less-lethal’ weaponry (and you can too)
sessions.description:
The nonprofit newsroom Evident teams up with the Human Rights Center at UC Berkeley to present their visual investigation into a controversial weapon used by police on the streets of American cities. This session will pull back the curtain on the research and storytelling process, featuring documentary storytelling, data visualization, and a range of dynamic visual journalism. The team behind the project will also offer guidance and ideas for citizen journalism to cover police use of less-lethal weaponry.

BUY A STANDALONE TICKET
sessions.venue: The Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg Center
sessions.page_title: Visual Investigation Breakdown: How Evident revealed dangers of ‘less-lethal’ weaponry (and you can too)

sessions.title: Rights on Paper, Risk on the Ground
sessions.description:
Citizens who take on the work of journalism rarely have an institution or a legal team standing behind them when things go sideways. This workshop is built for that gap — covering both what the law actually protects and what it takes to stay safe in the moment when protection isn’t guaranteed. Participants work through real scenarios: securing devices and communications, recognizing the lines of the reporter’s role, documenting encounters with law enforcement, and reading a situation in real time.

What you’ll leave with: a working understanding of your rights on paper, how to judge what’s safe on the ground, and how to mitigate risk when you’re on your own.

BUY A STANDALONE TICKET
sessions.venue: The Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg Center
sessions.page_title: Rights on Paper, Risk on the Ground

sessions.title: Rights from the Ground Up
sessions.description:
The rights journalists exercise — to film in public, to request government records, to refuse to identify sources — belong to every citizen. But unlike professional journalists, whose rights are defended by the in-house counsel, the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, the Committee to Protect Journalists, and a network of other press freedom organizations, ordinary citizens face the consequences of exercising those rights largely alone. As government conduct has grown more aggressive — masked immigration agents, surveillance of protesters, retaliation against public employees who speak out — the gap between legal rights and practical protection has widened dangerously.
